titre: Citizen Kane didn't fail in 1941; it was made to fail
accroche: Hollywood studios offer RKO more than $800,000 to buy the negative of the film and burn it before it reaches theaters.
contenu_vulgarise:
Orson Welles is twenty-four when he takes on William Randolph Hearst with Citizen Kane, a barely disguised portrait of the press magnate in the guise of Charles Foster Kane. The film is released in 1941. At the private screenings that precede its release, nearly every viewer recognizes a masterpiece, with one exception: the columnist Hedda Hopper, who immediately warns Hearst. Furious, he commits every resource of his press empire to keeping the film from existing.

## Buying the film to destroy it

Her fellow columnist Louella Parsons, another feared gossip writer, takes it upon herself to rally the Hollywood studios against Welles. Louis B. Mayer, head of MGM, leads a coalition of studios that offer RKO president George Schaefer more than eight hundred thousand dollars in exchange for the outright destruction of the negative and all prints of the film, a sum that would have covered RKO's initial investment. Schaefer refuses, backed by the financier Nelson Rockefeller, and in turn threatens a lawsuit. The coalition backs down.

Hearst doesn't stop there. His newspapers threaten to dredge up old Hollywood scandals they had until then smothered at the studios' request, insinuate that Welles is a communist who refuses to serve his country, and his supporters pressure theater owners to turn the film away. Several major theater chains simply drop it from their programming.

The result shows at the 1942 Oscars: nominated in nine categories, including Best Picture, Citizen Kane walks away with just one statuette, Best Original Screenplay, shared by Welles and Herman Mankiewicz. The film then quietly goes back into RKO's vaults. It will take nearly a quarter century, and its rediscovery by a new generation of critics, before it is recognized as one of the greatest films in the history of cinema.

## What this shifts

Nothing in this story comes down to a disagreement over the film's quality: those who saw it before its release, including its most determined opponents, knew they were dealing with a triumph. What the eight lost nominations measure is therefore not an aesthetic judgment, but the effectiveness of a campaign run from newsrooms, studios and the theaters themselves. It took an entire generation of viewers who had never known Hearst rediscovering the film, in the 1950s and 1960s, for Citizen Kane to get the place its 1941 release had denied it.

carte.punch: Studios offered RKO more than $800,000 to destroy the negative of Citizen Kane.
carte.idee: In 1941, William Randolph Hearst mobilizes his newspapers and a coalition of studios led by Louis B. Mayer, which offers RKO more than $800,000 to destroy the negative of Citizen Kane. The film will win only one Oscar out of nine nominations.

quiz.question: According to the documented facts, why did Citizen Kane win only one Oscar out of the nine categories in which it was nominated, in 1942?
choix: The film's final cut, finished in haste, had technical flaws noted by the jury
William Randolph Hearst had mobilized his newspapers, rival studios and movie theaters to discredit the film and intimidate its supporters
Orson Welles had refused to campaign for the film, judging Hollywood awards of no interest whatsoever for his work
RKO had withdrawn the film from the competition before the ceremony, at its distributor's request
quiz.explication: Hearst, of whom the film painted a barely veiled portrait, mobilized his newspapers, a coalition of studios led by Louis B. Mayer that went so far as to offer $800,000 to destroy the negative, and theater owners to smother the film. Nothing suggests an unfavorable judgment of its quality, which was on the contrary praised by those who had seen it before its release.
